passages.text: High-Throughput Sequencing of <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> microRNAs: Evidence for Frequent Birth and Death of <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> Genes

In plants, microRNAs (miRNAs) comprise one of two classes of small RNAs that function primarily as negative regulators at the posttranscriptional level. <sentence_start/>Several <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> genes in the plant kingdom are ancient, with conservation extending between angiosperms and the mosses, whereas many others are more recently evolved. <sentence_start/>Here, we use deep sequencing and computational methods to identify, profile and analyze non-conserved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> genes in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis thaliana</italic>. <sentence_start/>48 non-conserved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> families, nearly all of which were represented by single genes, were identified. <sentence_start/>Sequence similarity analyses of miRNA precursor foldback arms revealed evidence for recent evolutionary origin of 16 <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci through inverted duplication events from protein-coding gene sequences. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, these recently evolved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> genes have taken distinct paths. <sentence_start/>Whereas some non-conserved miRNAs interact with and regulate target transcripts from gene families that donated parental sequences, others have drifted to the point of non-interaction with parental gene family transcripts. <sentence_start/>Some young <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci clearly originated from one gene family but form miRNAs that target transcripts in another family. <sentence_start/>We suggest that <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> genes are undergoing relatively frequent birth and death, with only a subset being stabilized by integration into regulatory networks.
Introduction

Eukaryotes possess RNA silencing systems to regulate or suppress a range of genes, genetic elements, and viruses <citation rid="pone.0000219-Meister1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15372041" doi="10.1038/nature02873" count="1">[1]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Regulation by RNA silencing can occur at either the transcriptional or posttranscriptional level, although in both cases, silencing is associated with formation of small RNA classes with typical sizes of 21 and 24 nucleotides (nts) <citation rid="pone.0000219-Meister1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15372041" doi="10.1038/nature02873" count="1">[1]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0000219-Tomari1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15741316" doi="10.1101/gad.1284105" count="1">[3]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Small RNA biogenesis occurs from perfect or near-perfect double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) that arises by synthesis of self-complementary foldbacks, by bidirectional transcription, or through the activity of RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RDR) <citation rid="pone.0000219-Meister1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15372041" doi="10.1038/nature02873" count="1">[1]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0000219-Tomari1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15741316" doi="10.1101/gad.1284105" count="1">[3]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Processing of self-complementary foldback or dsRNA precursors to small RNA duplexes is catalyzed by complexes containing DICER [or DICER-LIKE (DCL)] proteins and dsRNA-binding proteins <citation rid="pone.0000219-Meister1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15372041" doi="10.1038/nature02873" count="1">[1]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0000219-Tomari1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15741316" doi="10.1101/gad.1284105" count="1">[3]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Single-stranded small RNAs then associate with ARGONAUTE (AGO) proteins in effector complexes <citation rid="pone.0000219-Hall1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16216572" doi="10.1016/j.str.2005.08.005" count="1">[4]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Hammond1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16214139" doi="10.1016/j.febslet.2005.08.079" count="1">[5]</citation>. <sentence_start/>For transcriptional silencing, effector complexes associate (directly or indirectly) with factors controlling repressive chromatin, including DNA methylation and histone modification enzymes <citation rid="pone.0000219-Chan1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15861207" doi="10.1038/nrg1601" count="1">[6]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0000219-Noma1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15475954" doi="10.1038/ng1452" count="1">[8]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Posttranscriptional silencing effector complexes can mediate irreversible cleavage, translational repression, or subcellular redirection of target transcripts <citation rid="pone.0000219-Meister1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15372041" doi="10.1038/nature02873" count="1">[1]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0000219-Tomari1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15741316" doi="10.1101/gad.1284105" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Chu1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16756390" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.0040210" pmcid="PMC1475773" count="1">[9]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Liu1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15937477" doi="10.1038/ncb1274" pmcid="PMC1855297" count="1">[10]</citation>.

The expanse of genetic information regulated posttranscriptionally by small RNAs is potentially large in animals and plants <citation rid="pone.0000219-JonesRhoades1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16669754" doi="10.1146/annurev.arplant.57.032905.105218" count="1">[11]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0000219-Rajewsky1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16736023" doi="10.1038/ng1798" count="1">[13]</citation>. <sentence_start/>In humans, for example, computational and indirect experimental evidence indicates that miRNAs regulate expression of up to 1/3 of all genes <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lewis1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="14697198" doi="10.1016/s0092-8674(03)01018-3" count="1">[14]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0000219-Farh1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16308420" doi="10.1126/science.1121158" count="1">[17]</citation>. <sentence_start/>In plants, far fewer mRNAs are directly regulated by miRNAs, although the direct and indirect consequences of miRNA-directed regulation are significant <citation rid="pone.0000219-JonesRhoades1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16669754" doi="10.1146/annurev.arplant.57.032905.105218" count="1">[11]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Mallory1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16736022" doi="10.1038/ng1791" count="1">[12]</citation>. <sentence_start/>This is due to the roles of a large proportion of plant miRNA target transcripts that encode transcription factors required for normal growth, development, hormone response, meristem functions and stress responses <citation rid="pone.0000219-JonesRhoades1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16669754" doi="10.1146/annurev.arplant.57.032905.105218" count="1">[11]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Mallory1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16736022" doi="10.1038/ng1791" count="1">[12]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-JonesRhoades2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15200956" doi="10.1016/j.molcel.2004.05.027" count="1">[18]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Rhoades1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12202040" doi="10.1016/s0092-8674(02)00863-2" count="1">[19]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Approximately 21 families of <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> miRNAs and their respective targets are conserved in Rice and/or Poplar <citation rid="pone.0000219-JonesRhoades1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16669754" doi="10.1146/annurev.arplant.57.032905.105218" count="1">[11]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Additionally, there is a growing recognition of significant numbers of miRNAs not conserved in Rice or Poplar, many of which likely arose in the recent evolutionary past <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lindow1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16159385" doi="10.1186/1471-2164-6-119" pmcid="PMC1249568" count="1">[20]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0000219-Lu2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15994906" doi="10.1105/tpc.105.033456" pmcid="PMC1182482" count="1">[24]</citation>. <sentence_start/>In some cases, these <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci formed through inverted duplication events that yielded transcripts with self-complementary foldback structure <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>. <sentence_start/>In fact, the genomes of <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> and other plants contain a wide diversity of non-conserved, local inverted duplications that yield small RNA populations ranging from highly uniform, DCL1-dependent miRNAs (e.g. <italic toggle="yes">MIR163</italic>) to heterogeneous collections of bi-directional short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) formed by multiple DCLs <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lu1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16954541" doi="10.1101/gr.5530106" pmcid="PMC1581437" count="1">[23]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Henderson1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16699516" doi="10.1038/ng1804" count="1">[25]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Slotkin1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15908951" doi="10.1038/ng1576" count="1">[26]</citation>.

Deep sequencing methods now provide a rapid way to identify and profile small RNA populations in different plants, mutants, tissues, and at different stages of development. <sentence_start/>We and others have used high-throughput pyrosequencing to analyze small RNAs across the <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> genome in wild-type and silencing-defective mutants <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lu1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16954541" doi="10.1101/gr.5530106" pmcid="PMC1581437" count="1">[23]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Henderson1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16699516" doi="10.1038/ng1804" count="1">[25]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lu3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16141074" doi="10.1126/science.1114112" count="1">[27]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0000219-Axtell1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17081978" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2006.09.032" count="1">[29]</citation>. <sentence_start/>In this paper, we identify and analyze non-conserved and recently evolved <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> miRNAs. <sentence_start/>The data reveal a relatively large number of miRNAs that are so far unique to <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic>, and suggest that many miRNAs are spawned and lost frequently during evolution.
Results and Discussion
New miRNAs and miRNA target transcripts

Small RNA populations from wild-type (Col-0) plants, from <italic toggle="yes">dcl</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">dcl2-1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">dcl3-1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">dcl4-2</italic>) and from <italic toggle="yes">rdr</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">rdr1-1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">rdr2-1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">rdr6-15</italic>) mutant plants, as well as from several tissue types of wild-type and <italic toggle="yes">rdr6-15</italic> mutant plants, were sequenced using picoliter-scale pyrosequencing <citation rid="pone.0000219-Kasschau1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17298187" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.0050057" pmcid="PMC1820830" count="1">[28]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Margulies1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16056220" doi="10.1038/nature03959" pmcid="PMC1464427" count="1">[30]</citation>. <sentence_start/>This yielded quantitative profiling data for several classes of miRNAs and siRNAs <citation rid="pone.0000219-Kasschau1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17298187" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.0050057" pmcid="PMC1820830" count="1">[28]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Procedures for sequencing in a multiplexed format, normalization across samples, normalization for multi-locus small RNAs, and viewing at the <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> Small RNA Project database (ASRP) ( ) were described <citation rid="pone.0000219-Kasschau1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17298187" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.0050057" pmcid="PMC1820830" count="1">[28]</citation>. <sentence_start/>In addition to the populations analyzed previously, small RNAs were profiled from non-infected leaves (15,826 reads), or leaves that were infected for 1 hr (18,368 reads) or 3 hr (10,363 reads) by <italic toggle="yes">Pseudomonas syringae</italic> pv. tomato (DC3000<italic toggle="yes">hrcC</italic>). <sentence_start/>In total, 218,575 unique small RNAs (663,312 loci), represented by 470,426 reads, were used in this study.

A computational analysis to identify new <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> genes was done using a protocol similar to that of Xie et al. <citation rid="pone.0000219-Xie1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16040653" doi="10.1104/pp.105.062943" pmcid="PMC1183402" count="1">[31]</citation> (Figure 1A). <sentence_start/>All small RNAs from the ASRP database (Set1) were used (Figure 1A). <sentence_start/>Briefly, all loci from Set1 that yielded at least two reads (Set2) were subjected to Repeatmasker <citation rid="pone.0000219-Jurka1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16093699" doi="10.1159/000084979" count="1">[32]</citation> and bidirectional small RNA cluster filters to eliminate siRNAs from repeat sequence classes. <sentence_start/>Small RNAs that differed at their termini by up to four nucleotide positions were consolidated and passed through a self-complementary foldback screen with settings as described <citation rid="pone.0000219-Xie1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16040653" doi="10.1104/pp.105.062943" pmcid="PMC1183402" count="1">[31]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Small RNAs from coding sequences and complex small RNA clusters, or that were not 20-22 nt in length, were eliminated, yielding 228 loci (Set3). <sentence_start/>These included 91 of 102 (false negative rate = 0.11) rigorously characterized <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> genes used as a rule-development and reference set (Table 1) <citation rid="pone.0000219-Xie1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16040653" doi="10.1104/pp.105.062943" pmcid="PMC1183402" count="1">[31]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Failure to identify miR398a, miR399a, miR399d, miR399e, miR399f and miR447c was due to a lack of sequence reads. <sentence_start/>Known miRNAs also failed due to length (miR163), an incorrectly predicted foldback (miR164b and miR167d) or because the <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> gene yielded bidirectional small RNAs (miR156d and miR161). <sentence_start/>Small RNAs from known <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> genes were then removed from Set3, leaving 79 unique small RNA loci (Figure 1A). <sentence_start/>Two loci that had each failed at one filter step were reclaimed manually due to their abundance and their dependence on DCL1 ( ). <sentence_start/>The 81 loci (Set4) were then subjected to a detailed foldback analysis where small RNAs from the same foldback were consolidated into a single prospective <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> locus. <sentence_start/>A particularly useful, although not absolute, feature was detection of miRNA* sequences, which arise from the opposite foldback arm during DCL1-mediated processing. <sentence_start/>Detection of miRNA* sequences reveals the functionality of the predicted foldback. <sentence_start/>miRNA* sequences were detected at relatively low abundance for most reference <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> families (Table 1).
Figure 1

Identification and analysis of <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> miRNAs and targets. <sentence_start/>(A) Flowchart for the prediction of miRNAs and their targets. <sentence_start/>(B) Validation of predicted targets for 13 non-conserved miRNAs. <sentence_start/>Positions of dominant 5′ RACE products (no. 5′ ends at position/total no. 5′ ends sequenced) are indicated by vertical arrows in the expanded regions. <sentence_start/>Predicted cleavage sites are indicated by a bolded nucleotide at position ten relative to the 5′ end of the miRNA or miRNA-variant. <sentence_start/>Positions of gene-specific primers are indicated with horizontal arrows above gene diagrams.

Thirty-nine loci (Set5) beyond the reference set emerged as prospective miRNAs, including 25 for which miRNA* sequences were detected (Table 2). <sentence_start/>Eight miRNAs from Set5 were detected recently as miRNAs by Lu et al. <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lu1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16954541" doi="10.1101/gr.5530106" pmcid="PMC1581437" count="1">[23]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Only one sequence, corresponding to <italic toggle="yes">Populus trichocarpa</italic> miR472 <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lu2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15994906" doi="10.1105/tpc.105.033456" pmcid="PMC1182482" count="1">[24]</citation>, was conserved in Poplar based on sequence/foldback similarity and target conservation. <sentence_start/>None of the new sequences were conserved in Rice. <sentence_start/>In several cases (miR830, miR833, miR851, miR861, miR862, miR863, miR864, miR865 and miR866), due to the ratio of small RNA sequences from both the 5p and 3p strands of the foldback, it was not clear which small RNA should be designated as the miRNA. <sentence_start/>In such cases, both the 5p and 3p strand sequences are designated (Table 2). <sentence_start/>In total, at least 70 <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> families were detected in at least one sequenced population (Tables 1 and 2, and references therein). <sentence_start/>Most miRNAs were lost or underrepresented in the <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> mutant ( ).

Target RNAs were predicted from both transcript and EST databases for the 39 miRNAs in Set5 by the method of Allen et al. <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>, which is based on additive, position-dependent mispair penalties. <sentence_start/>Seventy-eight or 69 of 85 validated, reference miRNA targets were predicted with a threshold score of 4 or 3.5, respectively (false negative rate = 0.08 or 0.19; Figure 1A). <sentence_start/>A total of 142 targets were predicted for the Set5 miRNAs, using the more conservative 3.5 score threshold (Table 2). <sentence_start/>These included targets predicted for both 5p and 3p strands for eight <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci. <sentence_start/>The 3.5 score threshold was used to maintain specificity, although at the cost of sensitivity, in the target prediction algorithm.

Top-scoring predicted targets for most miRNAs from Set5, and two that were not found in this study (miR778 and miR781) <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lu1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16954541" doi="10.1101/gr.5530106" pmcid="PMC1581437" count="1">[23]</citation>, were tested using a standard 5′RACE analysis to detect cleavage events at predicted sites opposite nucleotide 10 from the 5′ end of the small RNA. <sentence_start/>The 5′RACE assays were done using two gene-specific primer sets with RNA from whole seedling and inflorescence tissues. <sentence_start/>Thirteen targets for 13 miRNAs were validated, although evidence supporting miR775- and miR859-guided cleavage (At1g53290 and At3g49510, respectively) was weak (Figure 1B, Table 2). <sentence_start/>Evidence for miR846- and miR844-guided cleavage should also be interpreted cautiously, as targets were not cleaved at the canonical position. <sentence_start/>These were considered validated because both miRNAs had multiple sequenced variants that had predicted target sites encompassing the observed cleavage sites (Figure 1B; ). <sentence_start/>Additionally, targets for miR472 and miR774 were validated recently <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lu1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16954541" doi="10.1101/gr.5530106" pmcid="PMC1581437" count="1">[23]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Each target-validated miRNA was represented by at least ten reads or had a predicted miRNA* sequence represented with at least one read in the database, except for miR774 and miR778 which were not sequenced here (Table 2). <sentence_start/>Twenty-two predicted miRNAs that were sequenced at least two times, or that had miRNA* sequences represented in the ASRP or MPSS databases <citation rid="pone.0000219-Nakano1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16381968" doi="10.1093/nar/gkj077" pmcid="PMC1347440" count="1">[33]</citation>, failed at the target validation step (Table 2).

The relatively high proportion of target validation failures could be due to erroneous target predictions, low-abundance targets or miRNA-guided cleavage products, or low-abundance miRNAs with limited or no activity. <sentence_start/>Additionally, for 13 miRNAs, no targets were predicted at a score threshold of 3.5 (Table 2). <sentence_start/>While it is possible that many of these function to guide cleavage of unpredicted target RNAs, it is also possible that miRNAs exist without actual targets (see below).

Several new target families are worth noting. <sentence_start/>First, at least two targets are clearly under negative regulation by miRNAs in inflorescence tissue. <sentence_start/>Transcripts from <italic toggle="yes">AGL16</italic> (At3g57230, MADS-box) and <italic toggle="yes">MYB12</italic> (At2g47460, R2R3-MYB family) genes are targeted by miR824 and miR858, respectively, and are each up-regulated by 2-4 fold in <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">hen1-1</italic> mutants (Table 2, Figure 2A). <sentence_start/>Functions for these specific transcription factors are not known. <sentence_start/>Second, the transcript for the cation/hydrogen antiporter gene <italic toggle="yes">CHX18</italic> is targeted by both miR780 and miR856 (Table 2, Figure 1B). <sentence_start/>Dual targeting of the <italic toggle="yes">CHX18</italic> (At5g41610) transcript may lead to secondary, 21 nt siRNAs that arise through the RDR6/DCL4-dependent pathway (<citation rid="pone.0000219-Axtell1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17081978" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2006.09.032" count="1">[29]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15851028" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2005.04.004" count="1">[34]</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0000219-Yoshikawa1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16131612" doi="10.1101/gad.1352605" pmcid="PMC1221887" count="1">[39]</citation>; data not shown). <sentence_start/>miR856 may also target an unrelated transcript encoding the efflux protein ZINC TRANSPORTER OF ARABIDOPSIS THALIANA1 (ZAT1). <sentence_start/>Third, miR857 was validated to target the <italic toggle="yes">LAC7</italic> (At3g09220) transcript, which encodes a laccase family protein with predicted multicopper oxidase function. <sentence_start/>This represents the third miRNA family to target the laccase gene family <citation rid="pone.0000219-JonesRhoades2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15200956" doi="10.1016/j.molcel.2004.05.027" count="1">[18]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Schwab1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15809034" doi="10.1016/j.devcel.2005.01.018" count="1">[40]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Sunkar1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15258262" doi="10.1105/tpc.104.022830" pmcid="PMC519194" count="1">[41]</citation>. <sentence_start/>In fact, at least seven gene or domain families (encoding MYB, PENTATRICOPEPTIDE REPEAT (PPR), AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR (ARF), AGO, F-box domain, kinase and LAC proteins) are now known to be targeted by multiple miRNA families <citation rid="pone.0000219-JonesRhoades1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16669754" doi="10.1146/annurev.arplant.57.032905.105218" count="1">[11]</citation>.
Figure 2

Comparison of conserved and non-conserved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> families. <sentence_start/>(A) Effect of <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">hen1-1</italic> mutations on levels of target transcripts for conserved (black) and non-conserved (red) miRNAs. <sentence_start/>Expression data are shown for two validated or high-confidence predicted targets, if available, for each family. <sentence_start/>Arrows indicate targets for miR824 (<italic toggle="yes">AGL16</italic>), miR858 (<italic toggle="yes">MYB12</italic>) and miR161.1 (At1g63130, a <italic toggle="yes">PPR</italic> gene). <sentence_start/>(B) Numbers of gene family members for conserved and non-conserved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic>s (Tables 1 and 2). <sentence_start/>(C) Relative numbers of miRNA target family functions for conserved and non-conserved miRNAs (Tables 1 and 2). <sentence_start/>Only target classes that have been validated experimentally are included. <sentence_start/>Note that Table 2 shows many <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> families with weak or no predicted targets, and these are not represented in the chart.
Direct sequencing as a miRNA expression profiling tool

The primary purpose of this study was to analyze new <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, the data from multiple mutants and treatments allowed us to explore the suitability of direct sequencing as a miRNA profiling tool. <sentence_start/>This was done in several ways. <sentence_start/>First, the reproducibility of the pyrosequencing method was analyzed using two normalized biological replicates [Col-0 inf. 1 (35,666 reads) and Col-0 inf. 2 (42,917 reads)]. <sentence_start/>miRNA families represented in both samples by at least three reads were compared and yielded an 83% correlation (Figure 3A). <sentence_start/>This experimental approach is essentially a random sampling from a very large population of small RNAs and hence we anticipate that this correlation would increase with greater sequencing depth.
Figure 3

Expression profiling of <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> families using high-throughput pyrosequencing. <sentence_start/>(A) Comparison of most-abundant miRNA families between biological replicates of Col-0 inflorescence (inf.) tissue. <sentence_start/>Normalized reads for each miRNA family member were consolidated. <sentence_start/>Note that <italic toggle="yes">MIR159</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MIR319</italic> derived members were counted separately, even though they are frequently assigned to the same family <citation rid="pone.0000219-Xie1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16040653" doi="10.1104/pp.105.062943" pmcid="PMC1183402" count="1">[31]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Palatnik1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12931144" doi="10.1038/nature01958" count="1">[57]</citation>. <sentence_start/>(B) Fold-change of miRNAs in <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> inflorescence versus Col-0 inflorescence (left axis, bars). <sentence_start/>Total number of reads for each family is indicated (right axis, green line). <sentence_start/>As the <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> mutant contained no reads for many miRNA families, fold-change was calculated using normalized reads+1. <sentence_start/>This had the effect of dampening fold-change values for low-abundance families. <sentence_start/>(C) Fold-change of miRNA family reads in leaves at 1 hr and 3 hr post-inoculation with <italic toggle="yes">P. syringae</italic> (DC3000<italic toggle="yes">hrcC</italic>) (left axis, bars). <sentence_start/>Fold-change relative to uninoculated leaves was calculated based on normalized reads as described in panel (B). <sentence_start/>Total number of reads in the control and inoculated samples is shown (right axis, green line). <sentence_start/>Grey dashed lines indicate the <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.05 upper and lower thresholds.

We next compared normalized expression profiles of miRNA families in Col-0 (inflorescence tissues) and <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> (inflorescence tissues) mutant plants. <sentence_start/>As expected, based on the requirement for DCL1 in miRNA precursor processing, levels of nearly all miRNA families were decreased in <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> mutant plants (Figure 3B). <sentence_start/>A few miRNAs were largely unaffected in <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> plants. <sentence_start/>This likely reflects the known residual activity in, and the insensitivity of some miRNAs to, the partial-loss-of-function <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> mutant allele <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>.

To extend our small RNA profiling beyond different tissues and developmental stages, we generated expression profiles of miRNA families in leaves following infection by <italic toggle="yes">P. syringae</italic> pv. tomato (DC3000<italic toggle="yes">hrcC</italic>) at 0, 1 and 3 hr post-inoculation (p.i.) timepoints. <sentence_start/>This bacterium is unable to cause disease, because it is mutated in the key virulence factor delivery machine, the type III secretion system. <sentence_start/>This strain does trigger a robust basal defense response in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> <citation rid="pone.0000219-Jones1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17108957" doi="10.1038/nature05286" count="1">[42]</citation>. <sentence_start/>As predicted <citation rid="pone.0000219-Navarro1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16627744" doi="10.1126/science.1126088" count="1">[43]</citation>, miR393 was strongly up-regulated (10-fold at 3 hr p.i.) (Figure 3C). <sentence_start/>miR393 targets mRNAs encoding the auxin receptor, TRANSPORT INHIBITOR RESPONSE1 (TIR1), and related proteins <citation rid="pone.0000219-JonesRhoades2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15200956" doi="10.1016/j.molcel.2004.05.027" count="1">[18]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Navarro1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16627744" doi="10.1126/science.1126088" count="1">[43]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Two additional miRNA families, miR160 and miR167, were significantly elevated at 3 hr p.i. <sentence_start/>by 5-fold and 6-fold, respectively (Figure 3C). <sentence_start/>miR160 and miR167 each target mRNAs encoding members of the ARF family of transcription factors <citation rid="pone.0000219-Rhoades1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12202040" doi="10.1016/s0092-8674(02)00863-2" count="1">[19]</citation>. <sentence_start/>These data suggest that basal defense responses triggered by <italic toggle="yes">P. syringae</italic> pv. tomato (DC3000<italic toggle="yes">hrcC</italic>) include miRNA-mediated suppression of multiple components of auxin signaling pathways. <sentence_start/>Hence, our data extend the conclusions of Navarro et al. <citation rid="pone.0000219-Navarro1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16627744" doi="10.1126/science.1126088" count="1">[43]</citation>. miR825, for which several targets were predicted but not validated (Table 2), was significantly down-regulated 3 hr p.i. <sentence_start/>(Figure 3C).

Thus, direct sequence-based profiling shows considerable promise in revealing dynamic changes in miRNA populations, although shallow sequencing depth will limit applicability of the method. <sentence_start/>While both open-ended platforms (such as direct sequencing) and closed-ended platforms (such as solid-state microarrays) can be used to profile known miRNAs, the sequence-based profiling approach affords discovery of previously unknown miRNAs. <sentence_start/>It also allows discrete measurements of complex mixtures of small RNAs that arise in heterogeneous populations from loci with diffuse boundaries <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lu1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16954541" doi="10.1101/gr.5530106" pmcid="PMC1581437" count="1">[23]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Lu3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16141074" doi="10.1126/science.1114112" count="1">[27]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Kasschau1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17298187" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.0050057" pmcid="PMC1820830" count="1">[28]</citation>.
Conserved vs. non-conserved miRNAs

Twenty-two and 20 <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> families (Tables 1 and 2) are conserved in Poplar and Rice, respectively. <sentence_start/>Conserved families in <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> were designated by having identical or related (three or fewer nucleotide substitutions) sequences, and at least one conserved target transcript, in either Poplar or Rice. <sentence_start/>A series of general and functional comparisons between conserved and non-conserved families was done. <sentence_start/>Whereas 19 of 22 conserved <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> miRNA families were represented at multiple loci, only three (<italic toggle="yes">MIR158</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MIR447</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MIR845</italic>) of 48 non-conserved miRNAs were members of multigene families (Figure 2B). <sentence_start/>Expansion of multigene <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> families has occurred through tandem and segmental duplications, as well as polyploidization events <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Guddeti1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16117853" doi="10.1038/sj.cr.7290333" count="1">[44]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Jiang1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16699546" doi="10.1038/sj.cr.7310062" count="1">[45]</citation>. <sentence_start/>The preponderance of single gene families among the non-conserved miRNAs is consistent with recent evolutionary derivation.

Functions of conserved miRNA target genes, as a group, are less diverse than functions for non-conserved miRNA target genes (only validated or high-confidence targets were compared). <sentence_start/>This is due primarily to the high proportion of target mRNAs encoding transcription factors for conserved families (Table 1 and 2, Figure 2C). <sentence_start/>As pointed out clearly before <citation rid="pone.0000219-JonesRhoades2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15200956" doi="10.1016/j.molcel.2004.05.027" count="1">[18]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Rhoades1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12202040" doi="10.1016/s0092-8674(02)00863-2" count="1">[19]</citation>, the vast majority of transcription factor families targeted by conserved miRNAs participate in developmental pathways, including those specifying meristem functions, organ polarity, cell division control, organ separation and hormone responses. <sentence_start/>Non-conserved miRNA target genes encode a broad range of proteins, including a limited number of transcription factors (Table 2, Figure 2C). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, several non-conserved miRNAs (miR161 and miR400) target transcripts from a clade within the large <italic toggle="yes">PPR</italic> family <citation rid="pone.0000219-Rhoades1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12202040" doi="10.1016/s0092-8674(02)00863-2" count="1">[19]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Sunkar1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15258262" doi="10.1105/tpc.104.022830" pmcid="PMC519194" count="1">[41]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Another non-conserved miRNA, miR173, targets tasiRNA primary transcripts (<italic toggle="yes">TAS1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">TAS2</italic>) <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15851028" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2005.04.004" count="1">[34]</citation>, which in turn yield siRNAs that also target several of the miR161- and miR400-targeted <italic toggle="yes">PPR</italic> transcripts (<citation rid="pone.0000219-Axtell1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17081978" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2006.09.032" count="1">[29]</citation>; data not shown).

To what extent do the non-conserved miRNAs negatively regulate target genes? <sentence_start/>The sensitivity of target genes of conserved and non-conserved miRNAs was analyzed by transcript profiling in wild-type (Col-0 and La-<italic toggle="yes">er</italic>) plants and mutant plants with general miRNA deficiencies (<italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">hen1-1</italic>). <sentence_start/>To avoid biasing the analysis with miRNAs that target disproportionately high numbers of target mRNAs, such as miR161 and <italic toggle="yes">PPR</italic> target gene family members, the number of genes analyzed for each miRNA family was limited to two validated targets, or two predicted targets with the lowest scores. <sentence_start/>For miRNAs that have been shown to target multiple gene families, such as miR395, two targets from both gene families were analyzed. <sentence_start/>A scatterplot of fold-change in <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">hen1-1</italic> mutants for each target was generated. <sentence_start/>As shown previously <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15851028" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2005.04.004" count="1">[34]</citation>, conserved miRNA target transcripts displayed a generally elevated pattern in both mutants (Figure 2A). <sentence_start/>In contrast, most target transcripts of non-conserved miRNAs were clustered around the origin, indicating that most were insensitive to either the <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">hen1-1</italic> mutation (Figure 2A). <sentence_start/>The exceptions that were affected at levels of 1.6-fold or greater in either mutant included transcripts from <italic toggle="yes">AGL16</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MYB12</italic> and a <italic toggle="yes">PPR</italic> gene (At1g63130), which were targeted by miR824, miR858 and miR161.1, respectively (Figure 2A). <sentence_start/>While some of these data may be skewed by tissue-specific expression patterns of miRNAs and target genes, the general trend for non-conserved miRNAs having fewer effects on target transcript levels is clear. <sentence_start/>We suggest that, in contrast to the vast majority of conserved miRNAs, a high proportion of the non-conserved miRNAs are not integrated as dominant factors within regulatory networks.
Recent evolution of non-conserved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci

Previously, we identified a number of small RNA-generating loci with the potential to yield transcripts with self-complementary foldback potential and with extensive similarity to protein-coding gene family sequences <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Whereas the majority of these loci yield complex populations of siRNAs, two (<italic toggle="yes">MIR161</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MIR163</italic>) yield functional, non-conserved miRNAs <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>. <sentence_start/>This led to the idea that aberrant replication/recombination or transposition events from expressed gene sequences can spawn new small RNA-generating loci with the potential to evolve into <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> genes that regulate members of the originating family.

This idea was tested more rigorously with the expanded set of <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci. <sentence_start/>Foldback sequences for each <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> locus (Tables 1 and 2) were used in FASTA searches against <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> transcript and gene databases (Figure 4A). <sentence_start/>Nearly all foldback sequences from conserved miRNAs had hits with non-significant E-values greater than 0.05 (Figure 4B). <sentence_start/>In contrast, 19 of 48 non-conserved miRNA foldback sequences had at least one hit with an E-value lower than 0.05 (Figure 4B). <sentence_start/>Similarity or complementarity was detected on both 5′ and 3′ arms containing miRNA or miRNA* sequences.
Figure 4

Identification of <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> foldbacks with similarity to protein-coding genes. <sentence_start/>(A) Flowchart for identification of <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> foldbacks with similarity, extending beyond the miRNA target site, to protein-coding genes. <sentence_start/>(B) <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> gene or transcript hits in FASTA searches using foldback sequences for all conserved and non-conserved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci (Tables 1 and 2). <sentence_start/>The top four hits based on E-values are shown. <sentence_start/>(C) Z-scores for the Needleman-Wunche alignment values from <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> foldback arms with top four gene or transcript FASTA hits. <sentence_start/>Alignments were done with intact foldback arms (I), and with foldback arms in which miRNA or miRNA-complementary sequences were deleted (D). <sentence_start/>Z-scores were derived from standard deviation values for alignments of randomized sequences. <sentence_start/>In (B) and (C), a red symbol represents an experimentally validated target, a pink symbol indicates a gene from a validated target family, and an open symbol indicates a gene that is distinct from either the validated or predicted target family.

It is important to recognize that <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci contain two regions - the miRNA and miRNA-complementary region (largely overlapping with the miRNA*) - with relatively high levels of complementarity or similarity to target genes. <sentence_start/>To eliminate the potential misleading influence of these sequences, which may be under selection due to the requirement for complementarity between miRNAs and their targets, on the similarity test, each foldback arm with hits (E<0.05) in the FASTA search was analyzed independently with and without the miRNA or miRNA-complementary sequences. <sentence_start/>The top four FASTA hits (Figure 4A) were aligned with the intact or deleted arms using a global sequence alignment method (NEEDLE). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">MIR163</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MIR161</italic> were analyzed in detail previously <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation> and were included here as controls. <sentence_start/>Two foldback arm sets from <italic toggle="yes">MIR161</italic>, with miR161.1/miR161.1-complementary and the overlapping miR161.2/miR161.2-complementary sequences deleted independently, were analyzed. <sentence_start/>Sixteen foldbacks, including the <italic toggle="yes">MIR161</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MIR163</italic> controls, contained at least one arm with similarity or complementarity (NEEDLE score with p<0.001) to one or more genes when an alignment was done with both intact and deleted arms (Figure 4C, Table S3). <sentence_start/>For all hits with the deleted arms, the top-score gene alignments identified sequences that were immediately flanking the region with similarity or complementarity to miRNA regions (Figure 5). <sentence_start/>Further, in all cases in which multiple genes were hit with intact and deleted arms, the genes were closely related members of a single family. <sentence_start/>Thus, over 30% of the non-conserved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci show evidence of common origin with specific genes or gene families.
Figure 5

Similarity between <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> foldback arms and protein-coding genes. <sentence_start/>Each alignment contains the coding strand for 1-3 genes, the miRNA* arm, and the miRNA arm. <sentence_start/>Orientation of the foldback arms is indicated by (+) for authentic polarity and (−) for the reverse complement polarity. <sentence_start/>Two alignments are given for <italic toggle="yes">MIR824</italic> because the two arms are each most similar to distinct, duplicated regions within the <italic toggle="yes">AGL16</italic> gene (At3g57230). <sentence_start/>Alignments were generated using T-COFFEE. <sentence_start/>Colors indicate alignment quality in a regional context.

Interestingly, the two <italic toggle="yes">MIR824</italic> arms aligned best with distinct regions within one gene (<italic toggle="yes">AGL16</italic>). <sentence_start/>The miR824 arm was complementary to a region from exon VIII, and the miR824* arm was most similar to a duplicated region located within intron III. <sentence_start/>The two arms from <italic toggle="yes">MIR846</italic> were most similar to two adjacent but distinct regions of jacalin domain-containing genes or pseudogenes (At1g57570 and At1g61230). <sentence_start/>It is likely, therefore, that some recently evolved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci arose through juxtapositioning of sequences from two related duplicated sequences.

The protein-coding genes with extended <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> foldback arm similarity were analyzed in more detail. <sentence_start/>The intact foldback arms from 13 of the 16 gene-similar <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci were aligned with up to three gene sequences, and alignment quality was displayed using heat maps (Figure 5; <italic toggle="yes">MIR161</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MIR163</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MIR447c</italic> were not included). <sentence_start/>This revealed several sequence conservation patterns. <sentence_start/>For several <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> arm-gene alignments, including those containing miR778, miR780, miR824 and miR856 sequences, the aligned region containing miRNA sequences was clearly more conserved than the remaining arm segments (Figure 5). <sentence_start/>This suggests that selection may be operating on several of the recently evolved miRNA sequences, and is indirect evidence for functional significance of the miRNA. <sentence_start/>Indeed, miR824 targets the <italic toggle="yes">AGL16</italic> transcript, which is under miRNA pathway-dependent repression (Figure 2A).

For several other <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> arm-gene alignments, such as those containing miR862, miR447a and miR853, the miRNA-region of the alignment is similar to, or weaker than, the alignment containing flanking arm sequences (Figure 5). <sentence_start/>In fact, among the 16 <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic>-similar gene sets identified in this analysis (Table S3), only seven represented sets that corresponded to the best predicted or validated miRNA-target pair (Figures 4 and 6). <sentence_start/>In other words, nine of the miRNAs from loci with similarity to protein-coding genes were predicted to target transcripts from different genes (based on best target prediction scores). <sentence_start/>The target scores for eight of these sets were clearly weak or functionally implausible (Figure 6, Table S3). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, miR447a and miR856 were validated to target transcripts in gene families distinct from those similar to the foldback sequences (Figure 1B, Table 2; <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15851028" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2005.04.004" count="1">[34]</citation>). <sentence_start/>The miR447 family appears to have acquired novel target specificity and lost sequence-of-origin specificity, while miR856 may have acquired dual-targeting specificity (Figure 6, Table 2, Table S3).
Figure 6

Targeting specificity of recently evolved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic>s. <sentence_start/>Two target prediction scores are shown for each of 16 miRNAs: best overall predicted target score (blue) and target scores calculated for <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> foldback-similar genes (grey). <sentence_start/>Left column indicates whether or not the best overall predicted target gene is in the same family as the foldback-similar gene. <sentence_start/>A dot indicates that the predicted gene is in an experimentally validated target family. <sentence_start/>Two calculations corresponding to the two major populations from the <italic toggle="yes">MIR161</italic> locus (miR161.1 and miR161.2) are shown. <sentence_start/>The identities of targets are listed in Supplemental Table S3. <sentence_start/>The plot is centered on a target prediction score of 4, as this corresponds to the upper limit of a reasonable prediction.

The picture that emerges from analysis of the non-conserved <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> miRNAs appears to show that new <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci are forming frequently through duplication events. <sentence_start/>These newly evolved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci may first pass through a stage in which heterogeneous populations of siRNA-like sequences are generated, especially if the duplicated locus and resulting foldback sequence is large <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>. <sentence_start/>This, of course, assumes that the newly spawned sequence is proximal to a functional promoter. <sentence_start/>Computational evidence indicates that formation of <italic toggle="yes">MIR163</italic> through inverted duplication of SAMT methyltransferase-like sequences also involved duplication of the gene-of-origin promoter <citation rid="pone.0000219-Wang1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16901935" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btl437" count="1">[46]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Given that DCL1 has limited or insignificant activity on perfectly-paired dsRNA, acquisition of DCL1-dependence and subsequent formation of discrete small RNA products from the foldback precursor may require accumulation of drift mutations that result in foldback mispairs. <sentence_start/>From this point, we envision three evolutionary fates. <sentence_start/>The first and perhaps most common is continued sequence drift through mutation, decay of both targeting capacity and promoter (if not required for other functions) sequences, and eventual death of the locus. <sentence_start/>New <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> genes with neutral effects are predicted to take this route. <sentence_start/>The second fate is stabilization of the miRNA-generating sequence with specificity for gene-of-origin, or family-of-origin, sequences. <sentence_start/>This would occur if an advantage is realized when the target gene or genes are brought under negative regulation by the miRNA, and would lead to selection of the miRNA sequence. <sentence_start/>The miR824-<italic toggle="yes">AGL16</italic> regulatory pair may exemplify this evolutionary track. <sentence_start/>The third fate is chance acquisition of targeting specificity for a novel target gene or family, followed by stabilization through selection in the event of an advantage. <sentence_start/>miR856, which may target transcripts from both gene-of-origin (<italic toggle="yes">ZAT1</italic>) and a novel gene (<italic toggle="yes">CHX18</italic>), could conceivably fall into this category, although it should be noted that there are no direct data supporting a functional role for miR856. <sentence_start/>We postulate that many of the conserved <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> genes arose through the latter two routes, and have lost sequence relatedness to their genetic origin loci due to drift of foldback arm sequences outside of the miRNA/miRNA-complementary regions (Figure 4).

While this paper was under review, an article from Rajagopalan et al. <citation rid="pone.0000219-Rajagopalan1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17182867" doi="10.1101/gad.1476406" pmcid="PMC1698448" count="1">[47]</citation> describing results from deep sequencing of <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> small RNAs (887,000 reads) was published. <sentence_start/>They identified and named 32 new miRNAs (miR822-miR853), and another 39 candidate miRNAs that were not named. <sentence_start/>Sixteen of the named miRNAs, and eight of the candidates, were identified as miRNAs in this study (Table 2). <sentence_start/>In this paper, 16 miRNAs (miR845b, miR856-miR870) were named, eight of which were identified only here (Table 2). <sentence_start/>Differences in tissue sampling and sequencing depth likely account for most of the differences in miRNAs identified between the two studies.

). <sentence_start/>Col-0 (control for <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic>) and <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic> data were from experiments described in Xie et al. <citation rid="pone.0000219-Xie2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16129836" doi="10.1073/pnas.0506426102" pmcid="PMC1200315" count="1">[38]</citation> (GEO accession , samples , , , , and ), and La-<italic toggle="yes">er</italic> (control for <italic toggle="yes">hen1-1</italic>) and <italic toggle="yes">hen1-1</italic> data were from Allen et al. <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15851028" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2005.04.004" count="1">[34]</citation> (GEO accession , samples , , , , and ).
Small RNA libraries and ASRP database

Small RNA libraries and database construction were described by Kasschau et al. <citation rid="pone.0000219-Kasschau1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17298187" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.0050057" pmcid="PMC1820830" count="1">[28]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Briefly, small RNA analysis for wild-type (Col-0), <italic toggle="yes">dcl1-7</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">dcl2-1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">dcl3-1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">dcl4-2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">rdr1-1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">rdr2-1</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">rdr6-15</italic> inflorescence tissue was done by picoliter-scale pyrosequencing (454 Life Sciences <citation rid="pone.0000219-Margulies1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16056220" doi="10.1038/nature03959" pmcid="PMC1464427" count="1">[30]</citation>). <sentence_start/>Small RNA preparations from Col-0 and <italic toggle="yes">rdr6-15</italic> whole seedling, and leaf samples of Col-0 that were either uninoculated or inoculated by <italic toggle="yes">P. syringae</italic> pv. tomato (DC3000<italic toggle="yes">hrcC</italic>) for 1 hr and 3 hr, were also analyzed. <sentence_start/>Methods for normalization of reads were described previously <citation rid="pone.0000219-Kasschau1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17298187" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.0050057" pmcid="PMC1820830" count="1">[28]</citation>. <sentence_start/>All small RNA sequences are available for download GEO accession and the ASRP Database ( ).
miRNA identification and target prediction

A set of computational filters based on those developed by Xie et al. <citation rid="pone.0000219-Xie1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16040653" doi="10.1104/pp.105.062943" pmcid="PMC1183402" count="1">[31]</citation> were used to identify new miRNAs from among sequences in the ASRP database ( ), but with the following modifications. <sentence_start/>First, only small RNAs that were represented by two or more reads were considered. <sentence_start/>Second, small RNAs arising from repeat elements <citation rid="pone.0000219-Jurka1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16093699" doi="10.1159/000084979" count="1">[32]</citation> and bidirectional siRNA clusters <citation rid="pone.0000219-Kasschau1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17298187" doi="10.1371/journal.pbio.0050057" pmcid="PMC1820830" count="1">[28]</citation> were removed. <sentence_start/>Third, computational assessment of foldback structure was done with sequences containing 250 nts on each side of candidate miRNAs using RNAfold, Vienna RNA package, version 1.6.1 <citation rid="pone.0000219-Hofacker1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12824340" doi="10.1093/nar/gkg599" pmcid="PMC169005" count="1">[52]</citation>.

miRNA targets were computationally predicted as described <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15851028" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2005.04.004" count="1">[34]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Briefly, potential targets from FASTA searches (+15/−10 match/mismatch scoring ratio, -16 gap penalty and a RNA scoring matrix) were scored using a position-dependent, mispair penalty system <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15851028" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2005.04.004" count="1">[34]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Penalties were assessed for mismatches, bulges, and gaps (+1 per position) and G∶U pairs (+0.5 per position). <sentence_start/>Penalties were doubled if the mismatch, bulge, gap, or G∶U pair occurred at positions 2 to 13 relative to the 5′ end of the miRNA. <sentence_start/>Only one single-nt bulge or single-nt gap was allowed. <sentence_start/>Based on a reference set of validated miRNA targets, only predicted targets with scores of four or less were considered reasonable. <sentence_start/>Conservation between <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> and Poplar (<italic toggle="yes">P. trichocarpa</italic>) was assessed by FASTA search, foldback analysis, and detection of similar target sequences <citation rid="pone.0000219-JonesRhoades2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15200956" doi="10.1016/j.molcel.2004.05.027" count="1">[18]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Reinhart1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12101121" doi="10.1101/gad.1004402" pmcid="PMC186362" count="1">[48]</citation>.
miRNA target validation assays

Target validation using a 5′ RACE assay was done with the GeneRacer Kit (Invitrogen, CA) as described previously <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15851028" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2005.04.004" count="1">[34]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Kasschau2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12586064" doi="10.1016/s1534-5807(03)00025-x" count="1">[53]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Llave1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12242443" doi="10.1126/science.1076311" count="1">[54]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Poly(A)+ mRNA was isolated from seedling (7 day) and inflorescence tissue (28 day, stage 1-12 flowers) of Col-0 plants, ligated to adaptor, converted to cDNA and subjected to two rounds of PCR amplification using gene-specific and adaptor-specific primers <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15851028" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2005.04.004" count="1">[34]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Kasschau2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12586064" doi="10.1016/s1534-5807(03)00025-x" count="1">[53]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0000219-Llave1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12242443" doi="10.1126/science.1076311" count="1">[54]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Amplified products were gel-purified, cloned and sequenced. <sentence_start/>Gene-specific primer sequences for miRNA targets that were successfully validated are shown in Table S4.
Foldback sequence similarity analysis

The sequences comprising foldbacks from all <italic toggle="yes">MIRNA</italic> loci (Tables 1 and 2) were identified using RNAfold. <sentence_start/>Foldback sequences were subjected to FASTA searches against the <italic toggle="yes">Arabidopsis</italic> gene and transcript databases <citation rid="pone.0000219-Allen1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15565108" doi="10.1038/ng1478" count="1">[22]</citation>. <sentence_start/>The 5′ and 3′ arms of foldbacks that had gene hits with E-values lower than 0.05 were individually aligned to the top four FASTA hits using NEEDLE <citation rid="pone.0000219-Rice1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10827456" doi="10.1016/s0168-9525(00)02024-2" count="1">[55]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Each arm was also randomly shuffled 1,000 times using SHUFFLESEQ <citation rid="pone.0000219-Rice1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10827456" doi="10.1016/s0168-9525(00)02024-2" count="1">[55]</citation> and realigned to each of the top four FASTA hits. <sentence_start/>The mean ±standard deviation of the randomized sequence scores was calculated. <sentence_start/>A Z-score was calculated for each arm-gene pair by subtracting the average score of the randomized sequence alignments from the score of the arm-gene alignment and then dividing by the standard deviation of the randomized alignments. <sentence_start/>This was repeated for arms in which the miRNA or miRNA-complementary sequences were deleted from their respective arms. <sentence_start/>The deleted arms were aligned with gene sequences in which the target sequence was correspondingly deleted. <sentence_start/>Intact foldback arms and most-related gene sequences were also aligned and viewed using heat maps with T-COFFEE <citation rid="pone.0000219-Notredame1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10964570" doi="10.1006/jmbi.2000.4042" count="1">[56]</citation>.
